{{Short description|Theoretical framework for planar Euclidean geometry}}
In 1932, [[George David Birkhoff|G. D. Birkhoff]] created a set of four [[postulate]]s of [[Euclidean geometry]] in the plane, sometimes referred to as '''Birkhoff's axioms'''.<ref>{{citation |last=Birkhoff |first=George David |author-link=George David Birkhoff |year=1932 |title=A Set of Postulates for Plane Geometry (Based on Scale and Protractors) |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |doi=10.2307/1968336 |jstor=1968336 |hdl=10338.dmlcz/147209 |hdl-access=free |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=329–345}}</ref> These postulates are all based on basic [[geometry]] that can be confirmed experimentally with a [[Vernier scale|scale]] and [[protractor]]. Since the postulates build upon the [[real number]]s, the approach is similar to a [[model theory|model]]-based introduction to Euclidean geometry.

Birkhoff's [[axiomatic system]] was utilized in the secondary-school textbook by Birkhoff and Beatley.<ref>{{citation |last1=Birkhoff |first1=George David |author1-link=George David Birkhoff |last2=Beatley |first2=Ralph |year=2000 |orig-year=first edition, 1940 |title=Basic Geometry |edition=3rd |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=978-0-8218-2101-5}}</ref>
These axioms were also modified by the [[School Mathematics Study Group]] to provide a new standard for teaching high school geometry, known as [https://web.archive.org/web/20130615062200/http://userpages.umbc.edu/~rcampbel/Math306/Axioms/SMSG.html SMSG axioms].
A few  other textbooks in the [[foundations of geometry]] use variants of Birkhoff's axioms.<ref>{{citation |last1=Kelly |first1=Paul Joseph |last2=Matthews |first2=Gordon |year=1981 |title=The non-Euclidean, hyperbolic plane: its structure and consistency |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=0-387-90552-9}}</ref>

== Birkhoff's four postulates==
The distance between two points {{math|''A''}} and&nbsp;{{math|''B''}} is denoted by {{math|''d''(''A,&nbsp;B'')}}, and the angle formed by three points {{math|''A'', ''B'', ''C''}} is denoted by {{math|1=∠ ''ABC''}}.

'''Postulate I: Postulate of line measure'''.  
The set of points {{math|{''A'', ''B'', ...} }} on any line can  be put into a 1:1 correspondence with the [[real number]]s {{math|{''a'',&nbsp;''b'',&nbsp;...} }} so that {{math|1={{!}}''b''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''a''{{!}} = ''d''(''A,&nbsp;B'')}} for all points {{math|''A''}} and&nbsp;{{math|''B''}}.

'''Postulate II: Point-line postulate'''.  
There is one and only one line {{math|''ℓ''}} that contains any two given distinct points {{math|''P''}} and&nbsp;{{math|''Q''}}.

'''Postulate III: Postulate of angle measure'''.  
The set of rays {{math|{''ℓ,&nbsp;m,&nbsp;n'',&nbsp;...} }} through any point {{math|''O''}} can be put into 1:1 correspondence with the real numbers {{math|''a''&nbsp;(mod&nbsp;2''π'')}} so that if {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''B''}} are points (not equal to {{math|''O''}}) of {{math|''ℓ''}} and {{math|''m''}}, respectively, the difference {{math|''a''<sub>''m''</sub>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''a''<sub>''ℓ''</sub>&nbsp;(mod&nbsp;2π)}} of the numbers associated with the lines {{math|''ℓ''}} and {{math|''m''}} is {{math|∠ ''AOB''}}. Furthermore, if the point {{math|''B''}} on {{math|''m''}} varies [[Continuous function|continuously]] in a line {{math|''r''}} not containing the vertex {{math|''O''}}, the number {{math|''a''<sub>''m''</sub>}} varies continuously also.

'''Postulate IV: Postulate of similarity'''.  
Given two triangles {{math|''ABC''}} and {{math|''A'B'C'&nbsp;''}} and some constant {{math|''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0}} such that  {{math|1=''d''(''A',&nbsp;B' '') =&nbsp;''kd''(''A, B''), ''d''(''A',&nbsp;C'&nbsp;'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''kd''(''A,&nbsp;C'')}} and {{math|1=∠ ''B'A'C'&nbsp;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;±∠ ''BAC''}}, then {{math|1=''d''(''B',&nbsp;C'&nbsp;'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''kd''(''B,&nbsp;C''), ∠ ''C'B'A'&nbsp;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;±∠ ''CBA''}}, and {{math|1=∠ ''A'C'B'&nbsp;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;±∠ ''ACB''}}.
